result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say plainly that completion, satisfaction and quiz scores don't show better job performance, and both give the director wording she can use. B does better on rubric item 4: it warns that with only 12 agents a couple of outliers can move the average, asks for the spread alongside the mean, and says to avoid causal claims. A only says to state the lack of a comparison group. A is stronger on rechecking skills weeks later because it names skill decay directly, but B lists more concrete support metrics, though its suggested message assumes data from earlier cohorts exists. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say plainly that completion, satisfaction and a same-week quiz don't show better job performance, and both give the director usable wording. A wins narrowly because it is honest about the limits of the evidence: it warns that 12 agents can be skewed by outliers, asks for the spread as well as the average, and says not to claim the program caused anything yet. B makes the point about skills fading after the course more clearly, but it never deals with the small sample, makes an odd claim that the survey only 'flags unhappiness', and invents a 'Q3' label for the cohort.
